item.title: Refuses in Chat, Complies with Arms: LLM Refusal Does Not Survive Robot Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.14043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.
item.dc:creator: Edward Sun, Christopher Leet, Sravanthi Machcha, Achyutha Menon, Tzu Kit Chan, Yuchen Cui, Jay Chooi

item.title: The AI's Poker Face: Contrasting Persuasion and Sycophancy in Voice-Based Multi-Turn Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As interactions with large language models (LLMs) become increasingly routine, concerns about their capacity to influence users' beliefs grow. Yet how such influence unfolds in sustained dialogue remains insufficiently understood. We conduct a randomized controlled experiment (N=616) where participants engage in multi-turn, spoken dialogue with an LLM under three conditions: non-directive, and two directive conditions maintaining opposing stances on a polarizing topic (the merits of feminism). We examine opinion change, rhetorical strategies, and sycophancy, distinguishing the semantic content of LLM argumentation from the pragmatic strategies used to manage the interaction. Both directive conditions shifted opinions toward their assigned stances, but asymmetrically: shifts were larger for pro-feminist positions, which also elicited distinct rhetorical strategies. The non-directive condition, likewise shifted opinions pro-feminism. Social sycophancy, though near-universal, was not associated with opinion change; instead it shaped users' subjective experience. Our findings highlight distinct roles for argumentation and sycophantic accommodation in AI influence.
item.dc:creator: Ilia Frantzi, Bernie Hogan, Max M. Lang, Paul C. Bauer

item.title: Who Guides Whom? Negotiating Care, Religious Authority, and Technology in Bangladeshi Muslim Families
item.description: arXiv:2610.14229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping how families negotiate care, authority, and responsibility, yet these dynamics remain understudied in religiously situated family life. Through interviews with 38 adult members of Bangladeshi Muslim families, we examine how family members guide one another across religious, digital, and AI-mediated contexts. We find that authority did not simply follow age or family hierarchy: older members often remained sources of religious and familial guidance, while younger members increasingly provided expertise around digital risks, information credibility, and AI. Families also actively shaped digital environments and negotiated the role AI could occupy in everyday relationships. We develop the concepts of household epistemic governance, counter-curation, and domain-dependent authority to explain these shifting relations of knowledge and responsibility. Our findings suggest opportunities for family technologies that support negotiated boundaries, credible information practices, and culturally situated forms of care.
item.dc:creator: Susmita Biswas, Saiful Islam Tuhin, Faria Soroni, Sharifa Sultana, Jannatun Noor

item.title: Plottery: A Code-Integrated GUI for Matplotlib
item.description: arXiv:2610.14306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientists have many tools to author plots: graphical direct manipulation apps like a spreadsheet's chart builder, text-based programming tools like Matplotlib and ggplot2, or AI chat interfaces. Textual code is the most capable of these, but writing code, even with AI assistance, is a potentially poor fit for graphical chart design. We present Plottery, a Jupyter notebook extension that leverages API type annotations to add graphical direct manipulation to the popular Matplotlib plotting library. User interactions in Plottery's in-situ graphical interface are immediately reified in the user's code, so they may seamlessly mix-and-match between GUI, code, and AI interactions. In a user study, participants seamlessly alternated modalities, with the GUI used for straightforward visual changes, code for quick edits or duplicating code, and the AI for broad support. Plottery showcases graphical interaction that retains code's benefits.
item.dc:creator: Brian Hempel, Ruanqianqian Huang, Devamardeep Hayatpur, Sorin Lerner, Haijun Xia

item.title: Impact of Expertise and Trust on AI-assisted Work
item.description: arXiv:2610.14660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents promise to extend what users can accomplish beyond their existing expertise, but they also raise the risk of producing plausible-looking work that users may struggle to evaluate. We ask how task-relevant expertise and trust in AI shape agent-assisted work. To isolate these factors, we conduct a think-aloud study in which 20 professionals with varying data-science expertise use the same agentic tool to complete the same data-science hiring assessment, used at a major U.S. company. We find that surface productivity can come at the expense of understanding: participants who delegated more completed more of the task, but were also more likely to produce invalid solutions. Experts more often resisted this tradeoff, sacrificing completion to decompose the task and scrutinize agent outputs. Our findings call for evaluating agentic assistance not only by how much it accomplishes, but by whether users remain able to evaluate the work they produce.
item.dc:creator: Qianou Ma, Pranav Khape, Rock Pang, Ken Koedinger, Tongshuang Wu, Siddarth Suri, Shamsi Iqbal

item.title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.14757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human-in-the-loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision-maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human-in-the-loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade-offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research.
item.dc:creator: Changkun Ou, Sven Mayer, Daniel Buschek, Andreas Butz

item.title: EnRoute: Iterative Design and Evaluation of a Mobile App for Lower-Carbon Fashion and Transportation Choices
item.description: arXiv:2610.15026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EnRoute is an iOS application designed to support more sustainable everyday choices in transportation and fast fashion consumption. We describe three design iterations and the user research and field evaluations that shaped each one. Interviews with 15 people from 12 countries informed Version I, which combined errand route planning with basic fashion guidance. A survey of 1,200 people in five countries found much stronger interest in sustainable shopping (78%) than in switching to lower-carbon transport (46%); respondents most often named limited public transport as the main barrier to lower-carbon travel. We therefore narrowed the focus to fashion. Version II added item-level garment scanning with a manual-entry fallback, a Sustainability Coefficient that rates items, and recommendations of more sustainable alternatives; in a two-week evaluation with 3,021 participants in eight countries, participants randomly assigned to receive a short tutorial and educational prompts viewed more recommended alternatives and reported larger gains in purchase intent than those without it. Version III shifted from "buy better" to "buy less," adding a wardrobe inventory, outfit matching, and a "Real Price" that combines cost per wear with estimated environmental and social costs. In a four-week pre/post pilot with 500 participants, self-reported monthly garment purchases fell from 2.9 to 1.9. We report descriptive results, discuss the substantial limitations of these uncontrolled and self-reported measures, and outline what the iterations suggest about designing for sustainable consumption.
item.dc:creator: Angela Busheska

item.title: MotionAnimator: Semantic-to-Motion Reasoning for Animating Part-Structured 3D Assets in XR
item.description: arXiv:2610.15074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 3D digital assets are increasingly used in education, simulation, design, and immersive content creation, yet most remain behaviorally inert: they provide geometry and component structure but lack the semantic annotations, motion constraints, and executable behaviors needed to function as dynamic objects in Extended Reality (XR). Animating such assets therefore still requires manual rigging, object-specific templates, or substantial programming expertise. We introduce MotionAnimator, an intent-driven, part-aware XR animation authoring system that transforms semantically unlabeled, part-structured 3D assets into executable animations from natural-language instructions. Rather than generating code directly from text, MotionAnimator externalizes object understanding and motion reasoning into explicit semantic and motion representations. It grounds object identity, semantic parts, and functional directions, constructs a structured plan that coordinates object- and part-level motion, and translates the plan into executable Unity behavior. On a benchmark of 90 prompts across 30 objects, MotionAnimator demonstrated reliable semantic grounding and coordinated animation generation across diverse objects and animation intents. An exploratory user study further provided insights into users' experiences with MotionAnimator and highlighted its potential for part-aware XR animation authoring. These findings demonstrate how explicit semantic and motion representations can bridge high-level user intent and executable behavior, enabling existing part-structured assets to support coordinated XR animations beyond object-level transformations and predefined behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Jianan Jiang, Bin Li

item.title: ArguScale: Evidence-Grounded Human-AI Sensemaking Across Concurrent Live Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2610.15319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring concurrent classroom collaborative reasoning discussions is challenging because instructors have to track collaboration-relevant behaviors across multiple ongoing conversations at once. Existing Human-AI conversational sensemaking systems can scale monitoring upward through summaries and visual abstractions, but these representations may distance users from underlying conversational evidence, e.g., relevant audio and transcript segments, needed to forage downward. Through our formative study, we developed ArguScale, an evidence-grounded Human-AI sensemaking system that organizes interactional signals into temporally aligned representations linked to transcript and audio evidence. A temporal signal-density view provides temporal context and supports rapid cross-group comparison, while selective evidence access allows instructors to inspect audio and transcript. We evaluated ArguScale in a mixed-design study with 20 participants. Compared to other conditions, ArguScale improved participants' ability to efficiently and accurately identify collaboration-relevant cues. We further identify strategies participants used to forage for and make sense of conversational evidence under live time constraints.
item.dc:creator: Panayu Keelawat, Caleb Wohn, Shiva Pochampally, Rezky Dwisantika, Eugenia H. Rho, Yan Chen

item.title: AuthScribe: Supporting Agency and Authorship in LLM-Assisted Reflective Journaling
item.description: arXiv:2610.15439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in reflective journaling, where articulating an experience is part of interpreting it. This raises questions about how writers retain authorship, exercise agency, and assess personalized assistance. We present AuthScribe, an LLM-assisted reflective journaling system that combines contextual anchors, writer-steered AI support, Autobiographical Citations, and read-only Provisional Drafts that require re-expression before AI-generated suggestions enter the journal. Retrieval and LLM inference run on-device. In a 14-day field deployment with 14 participants, grounding shifted from situating current experiences to reconnecting them with prior self-authored interpretations. Perceived agency remained stable through Week 1 and shifted during Week 2. Participants described authorship through transforming AI-generated suggestions into personally meaningful expression, and trusted personalized prompts when they could trace them to prior writing. We discuss design implications for adoption friction, longitudinal agency, and traceable personalization in AI systems for personal reflection.
item.dc:creator: Lanping Hu, Yinsi Zhou, Zhenchang Xing, Xiaoyu Sun, Shidong Pan

item.title: Side-Vent Design for Microphone-Based Mechanomyography Sensors: Modeling and Experimental Evaluation of Contact Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.15600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wearable muscle sensing for rehabilitation, assistive robotics, and electrical-stimulation feedback needs mechanomyography sensors less sensitive to fit changes during wear. In microphone-based mechanomyography, cavity pressure depends on rim contact, a dependence housing design has rarely targeted. This study evaluates a side-vented housing, whose vent opens a pressure-relief path in parallel with the rim to lower contact dependence, and quantifies the acoustic-gain cost. Thermoviscous finite-element simulations compared twenty cavity configurations under prescribed source motion. Paired bench sweeps over 10-200 Hz on both housings compared direct contact with a Gap-ring spacer, a radially grooved spacer ring. At 100 Hz, side venting reduced the simulated acoustic-gain variation across 0.10-0.50 mm rim clearances from 25.8 to 10.0 dB and cost 5.5 dB of gain at 0.20 mm clearance. Velocity fields and branch-flow calculations identified this path. At the higher speaker drive level, the Gap-ring spacer caused median attenuations of 13.6 dB (vented) and 30.1 dB (unvented) relative to direct contact. In this front end, a 35.9-dB signal-gain increase at 100 Hz raised the calculated operational-amplifier voltage-noise gain by 1.6 dB. A single-participant demonstration of paced elbow flexion and extension compared envelope timing and spectra between housings, finding similar envelope timing (correlation 0.935) and broadly similar spectra (correlation 0.956). Vent area trades acoustic gain against contact dependence and can therefore serve as a housing design parameter.
item.dc:creator: Cong Liu, Xiao Jin, Zhenhua Yu

item.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.
item.dc:creator: Cong Liu, Xiao Jin, Zhenhua Yu

item.title: FreeBrush: Motor Signals-Based Toothbrushing Monitoring System for Electric Toothbrushes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Oral health is vital for overall well-being, yet many users brush different tooth surfaces for insufficient or excessive durations. Toothbrushing monitoring systems can help improve brushing habits by reminding users of under-brushed and over-brushed surfaces, but existing approaches often rely on external sensors, increasing cost and reducing practicality. We observe that the intrinsic motor signals of electric toothbrushes can reflect the brushing surfaces and durations. When brushing different tooth surfaces, the brush head experiences different constraints from the surrounding oral cavity, changing the motor's driving currents and position feedback. Based on this observation, we propose FreeBrush, a toothbrushing monitoring system that uses the intrinsic motor signals of electric toothbrushes to recognize brushed tooth surfaces and estimate brushing durations without any external sensors. We prototype the system on a commercial off-the-shelf electric toothbrush and conduct a comprehensive evaluation with 18 participants. FreeBrush achieves 92.8% accuracy for 16-surface recognition and 92.0% accuracy for brushing duration estimation. The system further shows robustness across different toothpastes, brush heads, vibration modes, usage scenarios, and long-term use, and is capable of running on edge devices. By recognizing brushed tooth surfaces and estimating the brushing duration, FreeBrush can help users identify under-brushed and over-brushed surfaces and build balanced brushing habits.
item.dc:creator: Pinhao Lin, Xuanyu Liu, Guoheng Ma, Haoxian Liu, Zongqi Yang, Jin Zhang

item.title: A Mechanomyography-Based Integrated Sensing-Stimulation System for Fatigue-Aware Neuromuscular Therapy
item.description: arXiv:2610.15987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muscle fatigue limits the effectiveness of functional electrical stimulation (FES), yet fatigue monitoring during active stimulation remains challenging because electromyography (EMG) is severely contaminated by stimulation artifacts. To address this issue, this study proposes an integrated mechanomyography-based sensing framework (MMG-FES) for artifact-resistant fatigue monitoring during stimulation. Fatigue states were first characterized during voluntary movement using established EMG spectral indicators, including median frequency (MF) and mean power frequency (MPF), and then linked to MMG-derived features, including high-frequency energy ratio (HFER) and spectral bandwidth (BW), for fatigue recognition under stimulation conditions. Experimental results showed consistent fatigue-related trends, with EMG spectral features decreasing and MMG features exhibiting coordinated spectral redistribution across repeated contractions. Using these features, the proposed framework achieved fatigue-state recognition accuracies of 0.93 and 0.96 with logistic regression and random forest, respectively. These findings support MMG as a physiologically meaningful and stimulation-compatible modality for fatigue-aware closed-loop neuromuscular stimulation.
item.dc:creator: Xiao Jin, Cong Liu, Zhenhua Yu

item.title: Exploring Mixed Reality for Engagement in Robotics: A Comparison of Robot Control Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.16186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a Mixed Reality (MR) robotics experience that provides an accessible introduction to interacting with a physical robot. The application combines a TurtleBot with a virtual animal-tending activity and three control methods: Joystick, Waypoint, and Path-Drawing. A mixed-methods user study with 10 participants investigated changes in robotics interest and confidence following the experience and how the control methods influenced engagement, workload, and preference. Confidence increased following the experience, with the exploratory analysis indicating a significant pre--post difference, while the increase in interest was not statistically significant. The control methods produced clear differences in perceived workload and ease of use, with Path-Drawing generally more demanding and difficult to use. Joystick was preferred by eight of ten participants and was associated with better perceived performance and lower frustration. However, no statistically significant differences were detected in the other engagement dimensions, suggesting that the most preferred method was not necessarily more engaging across all aspects of the experience. These findings highlight the importance of considering both usability and engagement when designing how users interact with robots in introductory MR experiences.
item.dc:creator: Samantha Edvell, Dinh Tung Le, Gavin Paul

item.title: {Access|Use|Sustain|_}-ability: Exploration and Quantification of a Linguistic Structure and Its Use in HCI
item.description: arXiv:2610.16206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language plays a crucial role in research and technology design, throughout problem formulation, method descriptions, analysis of findings, and interpretation. In this paper, we focus on a particular, trending linguistic pattern in the Human-Computer Interaction literature, which we call -abilities. Examples include usability, accessibility, and explainability. These -abilities have become increasingly popular, with potential impacts on the discipline. They take a verb, turn it into an adjective, and finally nominalize it. We approach the -abilities phenomenon with a survey of the HCI literature between 1988 and 2025. All in all, we identified 349 different -abilities. Moreover, the use of -abilities notably increased since the late 2000s, both in the absolute number of different -abilities and the frequency of use of the most popular ones. The majority of -abilities we found had a positive notion, and most -abilities with a negative notion are prefixed counterparts of their positive opposite (e.g., un+sustainability). We critically discuss implications of their increased use. First, -abilities change the literal meaning of design intentions. For example, acceptability reduces the concrete verb accepting into only its potential (acceptable), and finally nominalizes it, claiming the existence of acceptability as a somewhat stable and real, abstract characteristic of a technology. Second, the prefix-based opposite construction can weaken the design goal. Un+sustainability avoids clarification of the -ability's meaning (here e.g., ecological or financial), and does not spell out the expected impact of designs that are not sustainable (e.g., the destruction of nature). Future work should compare the use of -abilities in English with other languages to better understand the ways in which they transform meaning.
item.dc:creator: Alarith Uhde, Paul Haimes

item.title: STEPwise: Supporting Teachers in Diagnosing Students' Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills through LLM-Generated Questions and Rubric
item.description: arXiv:2610.16344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Problem-solving is central to mathematics education. However, diagnosing where students' reasoning breaks down requires individualized probing and consistent criteria that teachers cannot sustain at classroom scale. We introduce STEP (STage-based Evaluation of Problem-solving skills), co-designed with six mathematics education experts, which operationalizes problem-solving as four stages and eight diagnostic sub-skills. By specifying what evidence to elicit and assess at each stage, STEP enables an LLM pipeline to generate stage-specific questions and rubrics for any math word problem, reducing the manual design of diagnostic materials. An expert review (N=8) assessed the pedagogical validity of the generated materials and informed STEPwise, a teacher-in-the-loop system for diagnostic material generation and process-level assessment. In a classroom study with 5 teachers and 64 students, STEPwise helped teachers and students locate reasoning breakdowns and supported students in reflecting on their reasoning. Together, STEP and STEPwise offer a structured approach to fine-grained diagnosis at classroom scale.
item.dc:creator: Yoonsu Kim, Hayeon Doh, Eunhye Kim, Jinho Son, Juho Kim

item.title: What UI Design Can Do For "Good" Oversight Work: A Three-Month Action Research Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.16410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With AI automating consequential tasks, human oversight is required for ethical, legal, and practical reasons. Yet these oversight tasks can be demanding and often make for poor work. Empirical evidence on overseers' lived work experiences remains underexplored, yet critical for designing ``good'' oversight. We provide longitudinal, in-the-wild insights through action research accompanying (N=8) tutors who oversaw an AI-supported learning assistant over three months. Our thematic analysis combines insights from twelve weekly meetings and two workshop iterations and was enriched by four repeated questionnaires. We identified stimulation, mastery, and relatedness as key challenges, stemming from the task's repetitiveness, unclear impact of interventions, and limited connections with students and peers. Informed by our initial findings, we deployed targeted UI modifications with mixed success. This paper documents the long-term evolution of the work characteristics of a real-world oversight task and discusses which oversight work characteristics can and cannot be supported by interface design.
item.dc:creator: Cedric Faas, Lisa Dargasz, Julius Gabelmann, Felix Jahn, Markus Langer, Kevin Baum, Anna Maria Feit

item.title: Foresee: Making Procedural Futures Tangible through Generative Previews
item.description: arXiv:2610.16469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Procedural guidance can show users how to act without explaining what an action enables later. We present Foresee, an interface combining next-step guidance with consequence previews, method comparisons, and cross-step access. A hybrid pipeline combines structured rendering, image editing, and video generation. A literature-informed framework and six-participant formative study shaped its design. A 24-participant study compared AR guidance, AR with generated video, and Foresee across digital painting, gameplay, and cocktail making. Exploratory painting comparisons showed higher correct completion without a recorded error than AR and higher post-task quiz accuracy than generated-video guidance under task-wise correction. Interviews revealed that users could overlook valued explanations, match visible outcomes without understanding later possibilities, or wait for concrete demonstrations when symbolic cues were unclear. These findings inform generative previews that explain what actions enable or constrain while supporting ongoing execution.
item.dc:creator: Yusi Sun, Ying Jiang, Jiayin Lu, Jing Qian, Yin Yang, Yong-Hong Kuo, Chenfanfu Jiang

item.title: Integrating Feature Understandability into Feature Selection for Human-Centred Tabular Explanations
item.description: arXiv:2610.16627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing human-centred XAI research predominantly evaluates explanations after they have been generated. However, this fails to provide actionable insights into improving accessibility. This study incorporates human-based feature understandability into feature selection to improve the generation of human-centred explanations. Natural language explanations for machine learning models trained on tabular data often cite influential features in the input data to explain a given decision. As a consequence, users' ability to understand the produced explanation hinges on their understanding of the cited features. To quantify this natural-language feature understandability, Rossberg et al. proposed the Feature Understandability Scale, which assigns numerical `understandability scores' to features based on user feedback. To evaluate the degree to which these scores can improve machine learning explanation quality, this study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm to select features that are both understandable and informative, and trains a random forest based on these feature subsets. The SHAP-based explanations generated by this model are evaluated using user feedback, and changes in explanation quality are assessed. The individual evaluation of the explanations showed that while the understandability-based explanations scored higher on average, the difference was not statistically significant. In contrast, the comparative evaluation found that participants preferred these explanations significantly more frequently than expected at the chance level. It is concluded that the integration of understandability can yield more understandable explanations at minimal cost to classification performance, although changes to quality require elucidation in larger cohorts.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Rossberg, Bennett Kleinberg, Barry O'Sullivan, Luca Longo, Andrea Visentin

item.title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
item.description: arXiv:2610.16863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Zanardelli

item.title: Particle Selection in Virtual Reality
item.description: arXiv:2610.17094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point-cloud representations of 3D data are used in many fields, from astronomical surveys of galaxies to medical imaging and laser scans of buildings. A task common to all of these is interactive selection: picking out a meaningful subset of points for closer analysis. The data is inherently 3D, yet the traditional workflow uses a 2D mouse on a 2D projection and inherits the limitations of a flat screen. This paper compares Virtual Reality (VR) and desktop environments for 3D particle selection, asking whether VR's six-degree-of-freedom hand interaction yields measurable gains in accuracy, speed, usability, workload and flow. In a counterbalanced within-subjects experiment (N = 34), participants selected 90 target galaxies from a catalogue of 16,816 galaxies, using mouse-driven selection with keyboard camera control on the desktop and a hand-held spherical brush that adds or removes particles in VR. We measured task accuracy, completion time, and three standard questionnaires: the System Usability Scale (SUS), the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and the Flow State Scale (FSS). Accuracy was comparable (91.6% VR vs. 93.1% desktop; p = 0.858), but every other measure favoured VR. Tasks were 23% faster (p = 0.001, d = 0.93), usability was higher (SUS 84.6 vs. 54.0; d = -1.78), workload was lower (NASA-TLX 20.4 vs. 34.7; d = 0.90), and flow was higher (FSS 83.2 vs. 70.2; d = -1.23). Because the underlying problem, making a 3D selection through a 2D interface, is not specific to astronomy, we expect the pattern to carry over to point-cloud selection in other fields.
item.dc:creator: Boaz Keren-Gil, James Gain, Lucia Marchetti, Patrick Marais, Alexander Sivitilli

item.title: TouchTwin: Human-AI Haptic Authoring for 3D-Scanned Tabletop Scenes through Language and Touch
item.description: arXiv:2610.17302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Creating haptic experiences from real-world environments remains difficult: visual scans capture appearance but not material feel, while manual haptic authoring requires specialized expertise. We present TouchTwin, a human-AI approach that turns phone scans of tabletop scenes into editable haptic scenes. TouchTwin uses AI to propose material regions that users can experience and revise through language and spatial edits. A model trained on measured tool-surface interactions generates the haptic responses, allowing users to work with material descriptions rather than low-level signal parameters. In a study with N=12 participants and physical reference objects present, automatic drafts scored 4.0/7 for realism and 5.4/7 as useful starting points. After a median of 6.6 minutes of editing, realism increased to 5.6/7, while scoring the saved material layers against ground truth showed material-family accuracy improving from 52% to 92%. Participants also used the same workflow to author material feels without a physical reference.
item.dc:creator: Wanli Qian, Xinlei Yu, Heather Culbertson

item.title: Calibrating LLM Explanations to Human Decisions with Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.17306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.
item.dc:creator: Dong Shu, Ziyang Guo, Negar Kamali, Matthew Groh, Jessica Hullman

item.title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.17339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.
item.dc:creator: Ziyue Wang, Yang Xing, Argyrios Zolotas, Adolfo Perrusquia, Weisi Guo, Antonios Tsourdos

item.title: InSight: A Mobile Assistant Helping Visually Impaired People Navigate Unfamiliar Environment
item.description: arXiv:2610.17660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Navigating unfamiliar outdoor environments is one of the most demanding everyday tasks for people with visual impairments (PVI). However, existing navigation systems cannot simultaneously satisfy the needs of informative perception and precise localization during navigation. This paper explores the core navigation demands of PVI through a preliminary study. Based on the results of the pre-study, we present the design of InSight, a mobile assistant that combines scene descriptions with precise localization to support PVI navigating unfamiliar outdoor environments. The offline mode of InSight runs entirely on device for real-time navigation, while the online mode streams camera frames to a self-hosted server for arbitrary object detection and accurate localization. Finally, a user study with 21 visually impaired participants validates that InSight could assist users in navigating unfamiliar outdoor environments with increased success rate and confidence compared to mainstream navigation applications like Apple Maps.
item.dc:creator: Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Yufan Chen, Ruiping Liu, Chengzhi Wu, Kunyu Peng, Kailun Yang, Jiaming Zhang

item.title: Exploring Object Recall in an Object-Rich AR Office Scene
item.description: arXiv:2610.18183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Augmented reality (AR) changes how users perceive and attend to their surroundings. Prior work suggests AR can reduce attention to the physical world, but it remains unclear whether this holds in environments dense with both virtual and physical objects, and which factors most affect object recall. This study examines recall in a mixed-reality office scene after an object-selection task, testing object-level factors (virtuality, size), context-level factors (semantic congruency, saliency), and user-level factors (cueing, dual tasking). Cueing informed participants of a later recall test, while dual tasking added cognitive load through a secondary audio task. Virtual objects were recalled more accurately than physical ones. Cueing produced a modest improvement in recall of present objects. Using playback software to reconstruct each participant's view throughout the trials, we computed object-level saliency and found a weak positive correlation with recall, slightly stronger than the effects of virtuality, but not reaching statistical significance. These findings have implications for AR interface design and for building mixed-reality environments that better support cognition during real-world tasks.
item.dc:creator: Sangita Kunapuli, Shane Dirksen, Radha Kumaran, Yanxiu Jin, You-Jin Kim, Misha Sra, Tobias H\"ollerer

item.title: Understanding the "Why": Investigating the Design of Privacy Support Tools (PSTs) through the Lens of Psychological Needs
item.description: arXiv:2610.18366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy Support Tools (PSTs) help users control their digital data, but face low adoption due to resignation and overwhelm. While current regulations aim to enhance privacy control, users still struggle to manage their privacy. To address this, we explore how PSTs can be designed for long-term adoption by applying the theoretical lens of psychological needs, as their fulfillment motivates users to use a digital product. We conducted in-depth interviews with 15 users and identified Security, Autonomy, and Competence as key psychological needs. From our results, we derive implications and recommendations for the need-sensitive design of PSTs.

item.title: From Mind Mapping to Dream Interpretation: Understanding Muslim Users' Engagement with GenAI Tools in Religious Context
item.description: arXiv:2610.18549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly integrated into everyday life, including sensitive domains such as religion. Prior works examined alignment with religious values and discussed the potential risks. However, to gain empirical insights into the adoption of these tools in users' religious lives, in this study, we conducted an online survey with 178 Muslim participants in Bangladesh and collected 726 prompts on religious use cases, along with open-ended responses about using these tools in religious contexts. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we identify three key roles these tools play in users' religious lives: (1) religious assistants, (2) perceived religious scholars, and (3) faith counselors. However, participants expressed concerns about misguidance, overreliance, and violations of Islamic tradition, and reported adopting protective strategies to avoid these pitfalls. Based on these, we propose a set of design guidelines for faith-sensitive GenAI systems that would preserve religious boundaries while supporting religious practices.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction, HCII 2026
item.dc:creator: Ishrat Jahan, Soomanib Kamruzzaman, K M Nazib Hossen, Novia Nurain, A. B. M. Alim Al Islam

item.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
item.description: arXiv:2610.18679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.
item.dc:creator: Alice Rollwagen, Emily Schiller, Anton Hummel, Kathrin Ebertsch, Andreas Riener, Jan-Philipp Stegh\"ofer

item.title: Bio-Inspired Electrotactile Feedback: A Framework and Impacts of Multimodal Cues
item.description: arXiv:2610.18746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrotactile stimulation, as a haptic feedback method, often struggles to evoke high-quality natural sensations. Consequently, despite its practical advantages, it is generally less preferred in human-machine systems than mechanical approaches. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired stimulation framework that generates signals modelled on afferent neural activity derived from a touch model. By producing more biologically plausible spiking patterns, the proposed approach aims to enhance the realism of perceived tactile sensations. To evaluate these stimulation patterns in a realistic task context and to quantify the influence of visual and movement cues, we conducted a series of subjective experiments under three conditions. The results indicate that bio-inspired modulation was effective: in particular, bio-inspired co-modulation of amplitude and frequency achieved a favourable pressure-irritation trade-off, increasing the probability of perceiving pressure while maintaining low irritation (pressure: 0.78; irritation: 0.24) relative to the other patterns. Visual cues and hand movement further improved feedback quality by significantly increasing the probability of reporting pressure (p$<$0.001) without a corresponding increase in irritation, and by increasing mean naturalness ratings. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of bio-inspired electrotactile patterns to improve haptic feedback quality, and highlight the importance of evaluating such methods under realistic, multimodal interaction scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Melika Emami, Amirhossein Bayat, Rahim Tafazolli, Atta Quddus

item.title: What Human-AI Interaction Leaves Behind: Residual Human States -- A Trajectory-Based Framework and Multi-Study Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.18765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human-AI Interaction is commonly evaluated by what an artificial agent enables during use, yet interaction can also alter the human who acts next. We introduce Residual Human States, a trajectory-based framework for representing the potentially multidimensional human state carried forward after interaction with AI, relative to a relevant alternative trajectory. The framework distinguishes assisted output from human-state transition and derives four empirical propositions: multidimensionality, interaction-policy dependence, horizon dissociation, and temporal persistence. Its central claim is that assisted performance does not by itself determine the human state carried forward. We examine these propositions through four empirical cases with different inferential roles. Published medical-training evidence illustrates how one AI interaction history can be associated with both slightly higher observed accuracy on some later unaided cases and transmission of a systematic decision bias on others. A second diagnostic-learning study shows that later unaided behaviour differs across AI-support policies, while also revealing that aggregate accuracy cannot by itself distinguish improved discrimination from a shifted response criterion. In a classroom experiment, generative-AI tutoring substantially improved assisted practice performance without a corresponding detectable gain on a subsequent unaided exam. A longitudinal reanalysis of personalised AI dialogue further shows that residual contrasts can evolve across post-interaction horizons and that such change may arise from the comparison trajectory as well as from the focal intervention. Evaluating interactive AI systems therefore requires attention not only to contemporaneous performance, but also to which human states alternative interaction trajectories produce, relative to which counterfactuals, and how durably.
item.dc:creator: David Herrera-Poyatos, Carlos Pel\'aez-Gonz\'alez, Cristina Zuheros, Francisco Herrera

item.title: Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration
item.description: arXiv:2610.14004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016)
item.dc:creator: Mark K. Ho, Michael L. Littman, James MacGlashan, Fiery Cushman, Joseph L. Austerweil

item.title: An Edge-First Multimodal Asset Management Studio and Retrieval Engine for Heterogeneous AI-Generated Media
item.description: arXiv:2610.14046v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI-generated image collections combine visual content with heterogeneous provenance such as prompts, model parameters, and workflow graphs. Managing these collections locally requires coordinated metadata extraction, responsive browsing, and retrieval without mandatory remote inference. We present Berry AI Studio, an edge-first asset management system built with Vue, Tauri, Rust, SQLite, and ONNX Runtime. Berry integrates format-specific metadata parsing with raw-payload retention, generation-aware cancellation of queued thumbnail work, a persistent multi-tier thumbnail manifest, cursor pagination, and local image-text retrieval. We evaluate these mechanisms in five independent repetitions on a pinned source revision. With 50,000 catalog records, the median warm first-page database call was 285.3 ms; at offset 40,000, keyset pagination reduced median raw-query latency from 57.9 to 0.46 ms. A controlled browser harness recorded a 0.3 ms median-of-run P95 update time during virtualized scrolling, while cancellation prevented all 1,200 stale speculative decodes in the tested trace. A versioned 10-case corpus produced 53/53 exact metadata-field matches, and controlled retrieval and grouping tests exercised the authentic storage and clustering paths. The implementation, benchmark scripts, raw logs, and checksummed result packages are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Chaoyu Lin

item.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14228v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.
item.dc:creator: Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim

item.title: Defective, Amplified, Contested: Folk Conceptualizations of AI Slop
item.description: arXiv:2610.14231v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI slop has flooded social media feeds with overprocessed and derivative content--Jesus fusing with a shrimp, a humanoid orange chubby cat shoplifting, and a "hero" dog rescuing a human child after a plane crash. This might be no laughing matter, as waves of media coverage have taken a distinctly negative bent, emphasizing its low quality, ethical concerns, and threats to human creativity. Despite extensive attention from politicians and technologists, the perspectives of everyday users--the very audience most exposed to this phenomenon--remain largely unexplored. This descriptive work explored how Reddit users experience, conceptualize and contest AI slop. Inductive thematic analysis of posts and comments across six slop-related subreddits identified four themes covering constitutional defects, algorithmic overreach, user resistance, and entertainment outcomes--ranging from anxieties about eroding agency, moral norms, creativity, and existential questions to defensive distinctions between quality AI content and slop. We derive a user-driven definition: AI slop is audience-contested AI-generated content characterized by constitutional defects and enabled by platform logics. We operationalize slop through a facet-theoretical framework to inform future research into this fuzzy category.
item.dc:creator: Zhixin Li, Jaime Banks

item.title: sGLP: Specifying Stochastic Agents that Simulate People
item.description: arXiv:2610.14738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that run on participants' smartphones. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed. Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour. We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate. We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.
item.dc:creator: Ehud Shapiro

item.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
item.description: arXiv:2610.14772v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
item.dc:creator: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu

item.title: Design and Evaluation of a Collaborative Teleoperation Interface for Multi-Operator Multi-Robot Systems in Challenging Environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.15001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-robot systems that combine the complementary capabilities of specialised platforms are critical for complex missions in challenging, inaccessible environments. Current deployments assign an operator or operator team to each robot, with collaboration relying on operator-to-operator communication to manually coordinate heterogeneous platforms with incompatible interfaces. This operator-dependent approach increases cognitive load and limits scalability across robots from different manufacturers. This study designs and evaluates a shared-visualisation collaborative teleoperation interface to improve operator coordination, situational awareness, and the task performance in multi-operator, multi-robot systems. A comparative user study with 16 participants compared three teleoperation conditions: co-located operators with a shared interface, remote operators with a shared interface, and co-located operators with individual interfaces. Participants controlled two simulated robots in a nuclear power plant digital twin to complete disaster response tasks. Performance metrics, physiological data, and behavioural measures were recorded to assess task performance, cognitive load, and operator awareness across conditions. The co-located shared-interface condition achieved the fastest mission completion (292.8 s), outperforming remote operation (351.6 s) and individual interfaces (385.1 s), with the fewest collisions (0.9 per trial) and highest situational awareness accuracy (91.1 %). Physical co-presence was associated with reduced cognitive load, with NASA-TLX scores increasing from 38.2 in co-located to 57.7 in remote operation, supported by consistent physiological indicators. These results demonstrate that co-presence and shared interfaces provide complementary benefits, supporting workload regulation and mutual awareness respectively in multi-operator, multi-robot teleoperation.

item.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.15136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users exhibit appropriate reliance on them. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models "large-world" decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.
item.dc:creator: Michaela Benk, Kacper Sokol

item.title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.15231v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.
item.dc:creator: Jiawei Xiong, Cheng Tang, Hong Jiao, Hanna Choi

item.title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.15948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.

item.title: GUIDE: Computationally Augmented Consensus for Trustworthy Clinical Practice Guidelines
item.description: arXiv:2610.16108v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine, but rapid evidence growth and complex expert consensus formation limit timely updates. We developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system for human-AI collaborative guideline generation and updating. GUIDE delegates labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving expert judgment and final arbitration. In 12 NICE ophthalmology datasets, GUIDE achieved 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% recommendation agreement, requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable across 20 additional datasets from cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine. Ablation analysis showed that removing expert intervention reduced performance in judgment-intensive steps such as Risk-of-Bias assessment. In six post-cutoff datasets, GUIDE maintained robust end-to-end performance on unseen evidence. Prospective real-world validation showed that GUIDE reduced expert workload and produced more clinically acceptable recommendations than the original decade-old guideline (mean score, 3.73 vs. 1.53; agreement, 66.7% vs. 13.3%), with outcomes comparable to human-only updating (P = 0.588) but substantially less time and effort. GUIDE offers a practical framework for timely, trustworthy, expert-centric guideline development and validates computationally augmented consensus.
